recipes.title: Golden Turmeric Milk (Haldi Doodh)
recipes.description: Authentic Ayurvedic healing elixir crafted with spiced cow milk, golden turmeric, green cardamom, black pepper, and pure desi ghee.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Boosts vital Ojas, kindles Agni gently, promotes deep restful sleep.

recipes.chef_notes: Always add a pinch of freshly crushed black pepper to activate curcumin absorption by up to 2000%.

instructions.text: Pour milk into a heavy-bottomed brass or stainless steel saucepan over medium heat with turmeric and crushed cardamom pods.
Bring the golden milk to a gentle simmer for 5 to 7 minutes to let the botanical aromas infuse.
Turn off heat, stir in pure desi cow ghee and a pinch of black pepper; strain and sip mindfully while warm.

recipes.title: Moong Dal Paneer Khichdi (Sattvic One-Pot)
recipes.description: The most sattvic complete meal in the Ayurvedic kitchen — split yellow mung, fragrant basmati and fresh paneer simmered into a soft, tridoshic one-pot bowl. No onion, no garlic.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Classic Kitchari — the supreme Pathya Ahara. Easy on a weak Agni, rebuilds tissue (Dhatu) after illness or fasting, and clears Ama without depleting strength.

recipes.chef_notes: Dry-roast the moong dal for two minutes before washing — it deepens the aroma and makes the khichdi markedly easier to digest. Keep it loose; it thickens as it rests.

ingredients.name: Asafoetida (Hing)
ingredients.notes: sattvic stand-in for onion and garlic

instructions.text: Heat ghee in a pressure cooker, crackle the cumin seeds, then add asafoetida and grated ginger and let them bloom for ten seconds.
Stir in turmeric and diced carrot, then add the drained moong dal and rice. Toss for a minute so every grain is glossed with ghee.
Pour in 4 cups of hot water with rock salt, close the cooker and cook for 3 whistles on medium heat, or simmer covered for 25 minutes.
Release pressure, whisk the khichdi soft, then fold in the paneer cubes and let them warm through off the heat for 3 minutes so they stay tender.
Finish with coriander leaves and an extra half-teaspoon of raw ghee on each serving. Eat warm and freshly made.

recipes.title: Sprouted Moong & Peanut Protein Chaat (Sattvic)
recipes.description: Living food at its best — home-sprouted whole mung tossed raw with roasted peanuts, fresh coconut and lemon. A no-cook, no-onion, no-garlic protein plate.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Sprouting converts heavy Guru pulses into light Laghu food and multiplies Prana. Lightly steam the sprouts if Vata is aggravated or digestion feels cold.

recipes.chef_notes: Sprout tails of 3 to 5 mm carry the most Prana — beyond that the beans turn bitter. A 30-second steam takes the raw edge off without killing the crunch.

instructions.text: Soak whole moong for 8 hours, drain thoroughly, then tie in damp muslin and leave in a warm dark place for 8 to 12 hours until tails appear.
Steam the sprouts for 30 to 60 seconds if you want them gentler on Vata, then spread out to cool completely so they do not go soggy.
Dry-roast the peanuts until the skins split, cool, rub the skins away and crush them coarsely.
Toss sprouts, peanuts, coconut, ginger, green chilli and roasted cumin powder together in a wide bowl.
Add lemon juice and rock salt only at the moment of serving, fold in coriander, and eat within the hour while the Prana is still high.

recipes.title: Palak Paneer (No Onion, No Garlic)
recipes.description: Iron-rich spinach pureed silky and folded around fresh paneer, built entirely on a hing-ginger base in the true sattvic manner.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Rakta-building (blood nourishing) through leafy Tikta rasa, balanced by the Madhura sweetness of paneer so the greens do not aggravate Vata.

recipes.chef_notes: Blanch the spinach for no more than 90 seconds and shock it in cold water — this is what keeps the gravy emerald instead of olive. Never boil the puree after blending.

instructions.text: Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 90 seconds, drain and plunge straight into ice water, then blend to a coarse puree with the green chilli.
Warm ghee in a kadai, crackle cumin, add asafoetida and ginger juliennes and fry until fragrant, about 20 seconds.
Add the tomato with turmeric and coriander powder and cook down until the ghee separates at the edges, roughly 6 minutes.
Lower the flame, stir in the spinach puree with rock salt and warm it through for just 3 minutes — do not let it boil hard.
Fold in paneer cubes and milk, crush the fenugreek leaves over the top, cover and rest off the heat for 5 minutes before serving with bajra roti.

recipes.title: Kabuli Chana & Quinoa Protein Bowl
recipes.description: Slow-simmered chickpeas over fluffy quinoa with a cooling curd swirl — a complete amino acid profile in one bowl, built without onion or garlic.

ayurvedic_profile.dosha_balance: Pitta ↓ | Kapha ↓ | Vata ↑ (offset by ghee and hing)
ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Quinoa is light (Laghu) and drying, which stops the chickpeas from sitting heavy. The hing, ginger and ajwain together neutralise the Vata-provoking gas of Kabuli chana.

recipes.chef_notes: Rinse quinoa under running water for a full minute to strip the bitter saponin coat, then dry-roast it before adding water — the grains stay separate instead of clumping.

instructions.text: Cook the roasted quinoa in 1.5 cups water with a pinch of rock salt for 15 minutes, then rest covered for 5 minutes and fork it loose.
Heat ghee, crackle cumin and ajwain, add hing and ginger, then pour in the tomato puree with turmeric and coriander powder.
Cook the masala until it darkens and the ghee separates, about 8 minutes — this step alone decides the depth of the dish.
Add the cooked chickpeas with a cup of their cooking liquor and simmer for 12 minutes, mashing a few against the pan to thicken the gravy.
Season, squeeze over lemon, and build each bowl with quinoa at the base, chana above, a spoon of whisked curd and a shower of coriander.

recipes.title: Soya Chunk & Vegetable Curry
recipes.description: The single highest-protein vegetarian curry in the collection — textured soy nuggets simmered in a spiced curd and tomato gravy.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Brimhana and tissue-building, but Guru (heavy) and Abhishyandi. Best eaten at midday when Agni peaks, and always with warming ginger and ajwain to keep it moving.

recipes.chef_notes: Boil the chunks for 4 minutes, then rinse and squeeze them out three times in cold water. Skipping this leaves the raw beany note that puts most people off soya.

instructions.text: Boil the soya chunks in salted water for 4 minutes, drain, then rinse and squeeze them dry three times until the water runs clear.
Heat ghee, crackle cumin and ajwain, add ginger and green chilli, then add the diced carrot and sauté for 3 minutes.
Pour in the tomato puree with turmeric and coriander powder and cook until thick and glossy, around 10 minutes.
Fold in the squeezed soya chunks with a cup of hot water and simmer covered for 10 minutes so they drink up the masala.
Take the pan off the flame, let it cool for a minute, then stir in the whisked curd slowly so it does not split. Finish with cracked pepper and coriander.

recipes.title: Paneer-Stuffed Besan Chilla
recipes.description: Gram flour pancakes folded around seasoned paneer — twenty-seven grams of protein on a breakfast plate in under half an hour.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Besan is Kashaya and drying, which offsets the Guru richness of paneer. Ajwain in the batter is the traditional corrective for gram flour's tendency to bloat.

recipes.chef_notes: Rest the batter 10 minutes and keep it the consistency of thin cream. A hot pan wiped with ghee, then the heat dropped to medium, is what gives lacy edges instead of a thick pancake.

ingredients.name: Fresh Coriander Leaves
ingredients.notes: chopped, split between batter and filling

instructions.text: Whisk besan with curd, ajwain, turmeric, half the salt and about 3/4 cup water into a lump-free batter the thickness of thin cream. Rest 10 minutes.
Mix the crumbled paneer with ginger, green chilli, cracked pepper, the remaining salt and half the coriander.
Heat a flat tawa, wipe with ghee, pour a ladle of batter and spread it outward in a spiral. Lower the flame to medium.
When the top sets and the edges lift, scatter a quarter of the paneer filling over one half, fold the chilla over and press gently.
Cook 45 seconds a side until golden. Repeat for four chillas and serve hot with fresh coriander-coconut chutney.

recipes.title: Sattvic Rajma with Brown Rice
recipes.description: Kashmiri-style kidney beans built on ginger, hing and fennel-scented tomato rather than onion and garlic, served over nutty brown rice.

ayurvedic_profile.dosha_balance: Pitta ↓ | Kapha ↓ | Vata ↑↑ (needs the ghee and hing)
ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Rajma is the heaviest of the common pulses. Long soaking, discarded soak water and generous Ushna spices are what make it Pathya rather than Ama-forming.

recipes.chef_notes: Throw away the soaking water and add a small piece of kombu or a pinch of extra hing to the cooking pot — both cut the oligosaccharides that cause discomfort.

instructions.text: Pressure cook the drained rajma with fresh water, turmeric and the cinnamon stick for 6 to 7 whistles until a bean crushes effortlessly between two fingers.
Meanwhile cook the brown rice in 2.5 cups water for about 35 minutes, then rest it covered.
Heat ghee in a separate pan, crackle cumin, add the hing and ginger, then the tomato puree and coriander powder.
Fry the masala patiently for 10 minutes until it turns brick-dark and pulls away from the pan.
Tip the cooked beans and their liquor into the masala, add salt, and simmer uncovered for 15 minutes, mashing a ladleful of beans to thicken it naturally.
Crush the fenugreek leaves over the pot, rest 5 minutes, and serve ladled over the brown rice with coriander.

recipes.title: Panchmel Dal (Five-Lentil Rajasthani Dal)
recipes.description: Five pulses in one pot — toor, moong, urad, chana and masoor — for a broader amino acid spread than any single dal can give.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Mixing five pulses balances the individual excesses of each — the cooling Kashaya of chana against the warming Madhura of urad — producing a dal that suits nearly every constitution.

recipes.chef_notes: The second tempering poured over at the table is not optional. Ghee bloomed with hing and cumin right before serving is what separates a good dal from a forgettable one.

instructions.text: Rinse all five dals together until the water runs clear, then pressure cook with turmeric and 4 cups water for 4 whistles.
Heat 1 tbsp ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add half the hing, the ginger and the chopped tomato with coriander powder.
Cook the masala until the tomato collapses, then whisk it into the cooked dal with salt and simmer for 10 minutes to marry.
For the finishing tadka, heat the remaining ghee until shimmering, crackle the rest of the cumin and hing, and pour it sizzling over the dal.
Squeeze in lemon, scatter coriander, and serve immediately with bajra roti or steamed rice.

recipes.title: Tofu Bhurji with Bajra Roti
recipes.description: Crumbled tofu scrambled with cumin, turmeric and tomato, paired with iron-rich pearl millet flatbread — thirty grams of plant protein per plate.

ayurvedic_profile.dosha_balance: Kapha ↓ | Pitta = | Vata ↑ (bajra is warming and helps)
ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Tofu alone is Sheeta and Guru; pairing it with Ushna bajra and a heavy hand of ginger keeps the meal digestible rather than congesting.

recipes.chef_notes: Press the tofu under a weighted plate for 20 minutes first. Water is the enemy here — you want the crumbles to fry and catch colour, not steam in the pan.

ingredients.name: Pure Desi Cow Ghee
ingredients.notes: for the bhurji and the rotis

instructions.text: Press the tofu under a weight for 20 minutes, then crumble it coarsely with your fingers so the texture stays varied.
Knead the bajra flour with hot water and a pinch of salt into a soft dough; rest it covered for 10 minutes.
Heat ghee, crackle cumin, add hing, ginger and green chilli, then the tomato and turmeric. Cook until the tomato breaks down.
Add the crumbled tofu with salt and fry on high heat for 6 to 8 minutes without stirring constantly, letting some edges catch and brown.
Pat the bajra dough into discs between your palms and roast on a hot tawa, pressing gently until they puff. Smear with ghee.
Finish the bhurji with cracked pepper, lemon and coriander, and serve straight from the pan with the hot rotis.

recipes.title: Kala Chana Sundal (Temple-Style Protein Salad)
recipes.description: Black chickpeas tossed in a mustard and curry-leaf tempering with fresh coconut — the offering-plate dish of South Indian temples, and quietly one of the highest-iron recipes here.

ayurvedic_profile.dosha_balance: Pitta ↓ | Kapha ↓ | Vata ↑ (balanced by coconut and ghee)
ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Naivedya food — prepared without onion or garlic for temple offering. Kala chana is Kashaya and drying, strongly Kapha-reducing, and unusually rich in absorbable iron.

recipes.chef_notes: Cook the chana until it yields but still holds its shape — mushy sundal is a lost cause. Fresh grated coconut added off the heat, never fried, is the whole point of the dish.

instructions.text: Pressure cook the soaked kala chana with a pinch of salt for 5 whistles, then drain well and keep the cooking water for a dal or soup.
Heat ghee in a wide pan, pop the mustard seeds, then add urad dal and fry until it turns pale gold.
Add curry leaves, green chilli, ginger and hing and let them crackle for ten seconds.
Tip in the drained chana with rock salt and toss on high heat for 3 to 4 minutes so each bean gets coated and slightly dry.
Turn off the flame, fold in the fresh coconut, squeeze over the lemon, scatter coriander and serve warm or at room temperature.

recipes.title: Rajgira Almond Porridge (Amaranth Kheer)
recipes.description: Amaranth simmered in cardamom milk with crushed almonds and a whisper of jaggery — a sattvic fasting grain turned into a complete-protein breakfast.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Rajgira is one of the few grains permitted during vrata (fasting) and is a rare complete plant protein with lysine intact. Deeply Ojas-building when cooked in milk with cardamom.

recipes.chef_notes: Soak the almonds overnight and slip the skins off — Ayurveda holds the skin to be Pitta-aggravating, and blanched almonds blend far creamier into the kheer.

instructions.text: Warm the ghee and roast the rinsed amaranth for 2 minutes until it smells nutty and the grains separate.
Add 1 cup water and cook covered for 12 minutes until the grain swells and turns translucent.
Pour in the milk and simmer gently for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often so it does not catch at the base.
Stir in the slivered almonds and ground cardamom and cook 2 minutes more.
Take the pan off the heat, let it cool for 3 minutes, then stir in the jaggery — adding it while boiling will curdle the milk.
Top with ghee-roasted cashews and serve warm. It thickens as it stands, so loosen with hot milk if needed.

recipes.title: Masoor Dal Soup with Ghee-Roasted Pumpkin Seeds
recipes.description: A light, clean red lentil soup with bottle gourd and carrot, crowned with pumpkin seeds toasted in ghee for a zinc and protein lift.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Masoor cooks to a Laghu, easily absorbed broth — appropriate when Agni is weak or during convalescence. Lauki makes it cooling and gently diuretic.

recipes.chef_notes: Roast the pumpkin seeds in ghee only until they begin to pop, about 90 seconds. Any longer and they turn bitter and lose their sweet, green edge.

instructions.text: Pressure cook the masoor dal with lauki, carrot, turmeric and 4 cups water for 3 whistles, then whisk until smooth and broth-like.
Heat half the ghee, crackle the cumin, add hing and grated ginger, and pour this tempering into the soup.
Simmer the soup for 8 minutes with rock salt, adding hot water until it pours easily from the ladle.
In a small pan, toast the pumpkin seeds in the remaining ghee until they just begin to pop, then remove immediately.
Ladle into bowls, crack black pepper over the surface, scatter the seeds and coriander, and squeeze lemon in at the table.

recipes.title: Besan Kadhi with Paneer Pakoda
recipes.description: Silky curd and gram flour kadhi simmered slow, with soft paneer fritters dropped in — curd and besan and paneer stacking to twenty-two grams of protein.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Sour curd is Ushna and Abhishyandi — kadhi is therefore a midday winter dish, never a night meal. The long simmer and generous ginger are the traditional correctives.

recipes.chef_notes: Whisk the besan into the curd cold and keep stirring in one direction until it comes to a boil. Stop stirring too early and it will split every single time.

instructions.text: Whisk 1/2 cup besan into the curd while both are cold, along with turmeric, ginger and 3 cups water, until absolutely smooth.
Bring the mixture to a boil over medium heat, stirring continuously in one direction. Once it boils, drop to a low simmer and cook 25 minutes until it coats a spoon.
Make a thick batter from the remaining besan with ajwain, salt and a little water, coat the paneer cubes and shallow-fry in ghee until golden.
Slide the paneer pakodas into the simmering kadhi and let them sit for 5 minutes to drink up the gravy without going soggy.
Heat the last of the ghee, pop the mustard, crackle cumin, add hing and curry leaves, and pour the tadka over the kadhi.
Crush the fenugreek leaves on top, finish with coriander, and serve hot with steamed rice at lunch.

recipes.title: Badam-Dahi Protein Lassi (Sattvic)
recipes.description: Thick set curd blended with soaked almonds, pumpkin seeds and cardamom — a cooling, no-cook protein drink for hot afternoons.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Sweet lassi taken at midday pacifies Pitta and rebuilds Rasa dhatu. Diluting curd with water is what turns a heavy, Kapha-forming food into a light, digestible one.

recipes.chef_notes: Blend on low, not high. Over-blending heats the curd, kills the live cultures and thins the texture to something watery — thirty seconds is plenty.

instructions.text: Soak the almonds overnight and slip off their skins; soak the pumpkin seeds for at least 2 hours.
Blend the almonds and pumpkin seeds with the milk first, until you have a completely smooth white paste with no grit.
Add the curd, jaggery and ground cardamom and blend on the lowest setting for 30 seconds only.
Thin with chilled water to the thickness you like, pour into clay or steel tumblers and drink at midday rather than after sunset.

recipes.title: Protein Idli with Moong Sambar
recipes.description: Fermented urad and moong idlis paired with a lentil sambar — steamed, oil-free, and made genuinely high protein by shifting the batter ratio toward the dals.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Fermentation predigests the pulses and makes their minerals far more available. Steaming keeps the preparation Laghu, which is why idli is prescribed even for weak digestion.

recipes.chef_notes: Grind the urad dal cold and long until the batter is genuinely aerated — flick a drop into water and it should float. That float test, not the clock, tells you the idlis will be soft.

ingredients.name: Split Yellow Moong Dal
ingredients.notes: soaked 5 hrs, ground with the urad

instructions.text: Soak urad dal with moong dal in one bowl and the rice in another for 5 hours. Grind the dals first to a light, aerated batter using cold water.
Grind the rice to a slightly coarse paste, combine both batters with your hand, add salt, and ferment in a warm place for 10 to 12 hours until risen and faintly sour.
Grease idli moulds, pour the batter to three-quarters, and steam for 10 to 12 minutes until a skewer comes out clean.
For the sambar, pressure cook toor dal with lauki, carrot, tomato and turmeric for 4 whistles, then whisk in coriander powder and salt with 2 cups hot water.
Heat ghee, pop the mustard seeds, add hing and curry leaves, and pour this over the simmering sambar.
Rest the idlis 2 minutes before unmoulding, then serve four to a plate with hot sambar and coriander.

recipes.title: Baked Paneer Tikka (Sattvic Marinade)
recipes.description: Paneer marinated in hung curd, besan and ajwain with no onion or garlic, then baked rather than fried — twenty-one grams of protein for barely three hundred calories.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Dry heat cooking (baking) reduces the Abhishyandi, channel-clogging quality of fresh paneer. Ajwain and ginger in the marinade are what make a heavy Madhura food digestible.

recipes.chef_notes: Hang the curd in muslin for a full hour until it loses its whey. Wet marinade slides off in the oven; thick marinade clings and chars into that blistered crust you actually want.

ingredients.name: Lemon
ingredients.notes: half in marinade, half at the table

instructions.text: Hang the curd in muslin for an hour so all the whey drains away and you are left with a thick, cheese-like base.
Dry-roast the besan for 2 minutes until it smells nutty, then whisk it into the hung curd with ginger, ajwain, turmeric, coriander powder, pepper, methi, lemon juice and salt.
Fold the paneer cubes through gently so every face is coated, and marinate for at least an hour in the fridge.
Thread onto skewers, brush with melted ghee and bake at 220°C for 15 to 18 minutes, turning once halfway.
Finish under the grill for 2 minutes for char, then rest 3 minutes, squeeze over lemon and scatter coriander before serving.

recipes.title: Quinoa Upma with Sprouts and Cashews
recipes.description: A savoury quinoa upma studded with sprouted moong, curry leaves and ghee-roasted cashews — a South Indian breakfast rebuilt around protein.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Quinoa is Laghu and Ruksha, which suits a sluggish Kapha morning far better than semolina. Ghee and cashews restore just enough unctuousness to keep Vata settled.

recipes.chef_notes: Toast the rinsed quinoa dry until it crackles before any water goes in. That single step is the difference between distinct grains and a porridge.

ingredients.name: Fresh Coconut
ingredients.notes: grated, folded in at the end

instructions.text: Rinse the quinoa thoroughly, drain, and dry-toast it in a pan for 3 minutes until it smells nutty and crackles. Set aside.
Roast the cashews in a little ghee until golden and lift them out before they darken.
In the same pan, heat the remaining ghee, pop mustard seeds, add chana dal and urad dal and fry to a pale gold, then add curry leaves, chilli, ginger and hing.
Add the diced carrot, sauté 3 minutes, then tip in the toasted quinoa with 1.75 cups hot water and salt.
Cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, then fold in the steamed sprouts and rest covered off the flame for 5 minutes.
Fluff with a fork, fold in coconut and roasted cashews, squeeze over lemon and serve hot.

recipes.title: Til-Peanut Protein Laddu (Sattvic)
recipes.description: Sesame, peanuts and almonds bound with molten jaggery — the winter laddu of Makar Sankranti, and a calcium and protein dense snack that keeps for weeks.

ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: Til and gud are classically Ushna and Balya — eaten through Shishira (winter) to build strength and warmth. Reduce the portion sharply in summer or with high Pitta.

recipes.chef_notes: Take the jaggery syrup to the soft-ball stage and no further — a drop in cold water should form a ball you can flatten between two fingers. Hard-ball syrup gives laddus you cannot bite.

ingredients.name: Pure Desi Cow Ghee
ingredients.notes: for the syrup and greasing palms

instructions.text: Dry-roast the sesame seeds on low until they pop and turn one shade darker, then cool completely.
Roast the peanuts, rub off the skins, and crush them coarsely with the almonds and pumpkin seeds.
Melt the jaggery with ghee and a splash of water, and cook until a drop in cold water forms a soft ball you can flatten.
Turn off the heat, add the ground cardamom, then fold in all the seeds and nuts quickly and thoroughly.
While the mixture is still hot enough to handle, grease your palms with ghee and roll into 12 tight laddus.
Cool completely on a plate before storing in an airtight steel jar; they keep for three weeks.

recipes.title: Dal Palak with Sesame Tadka
recipes.description: Toor and masoor cooked down with spinach and finished with a sesame-cumin tempering, pairing plant iron with the vitamin C of lemon for real absorption.

ayurvedic_profile.dosha_balance: Kapha ↓ | Pitta ↓ | Vata ↑ (corrected by sesame and ghee)
ayurvedic_profile.therapeutic_note: The Tikta rasa of spinach scrapes Ama and purifies Rakta dhatu, while the dals rebuild it. Squeeze the lemon in only at the table — heat destroys the vitamin C that unlocks the iron.

recipes.chef_notes: Add the spinach in the last five minutes, not at the start. Long-cooked palak goes grey and metallic and drags the whole dal down with it.

instructions.text: Pressure cook both dals with turmeric and 3.5 cups water for 4 whistles, then whisk smooth.
Heat ghee, crackle cumin and sesame seeds together, add hing and ginger, then the chopped tomato and coriander powder.
Cook until the tomato collapses into the ghee, about 6 minutes, then stir this into the cooked dal with salt.
Simmer for 10 minutes, then add the chopped spinach and cook for just 4 to 5 minutes more so it stays green and alive.
Crack black pepper over the top, and squeeze the lemon in at the table rather than in the pot.

ayurvedic_properties.significance: Tridoshic in moderation. Powerful blood purifier (Rakta Shodhaka), anti-inflammatory, kindles Agni without aggravating Pitta, enhances Ojas and skin luster (Varnya).
Supreme Deepana (kindles digestive fire) and Pachana (clears toxins/Ama). Relieves bloating and abdominal cramps while calming Vata and Kapha.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Casein, Whey Protein, Vitamin B12, Riboflavin, Phosphorus

ayurvedic_properties.significance: The foremost Ojas-building food (Jivaniya). Best taken warm, spiced and alone — never with salt, sour fruit or a full meal, which Ayurveda considers Viruddha Ahara (incompatible).
One third of Trikatu, the classic digestive triad. Piperine acts as a Yogavahi — a carrier that dramatically increases the bioavailability of turmeric and other herbs.
Rare among pungent spices in being Sheeta, so it aids digestion without inflaming Pitta. Counteracts the mucus-forming quality of milk and clears the breath.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Butyric Acid, CLA, Vitamins A, D, E and K2

ayurvedic_properties.significance: The supreme Rasayana fat. Uniquely kindles Agni while cooling Pitta, carries fat-soluble herbs into deep tissue (Yogavahi), and is considered Medhya — nourishing to intellect and memory.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Casein, Conjugated Linoleic Acid, Phosphorus, Vitamin B12

ayurvedic_properties.significance: Brimhana — builds bulk and strength quickly, valuable for depleted Vata types. Guru (heavy) and Abhishyandi, so it needs ginger, pepper or ajwain and belongs at midday, not at night.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Lactobacillus cultures, Casein, Vitamin B12, Riboflavin

ayurvedic_properties.significance: Grahi and strengthening, but classically forbidden at night and in spring. Whisking with water into buttermilk (Takra) transforms it into one of the lightest and most digestible foods there is.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Lysine, Folate, Magnesium, Potassium, Resistant Starch

ayurvedic_properties.significance: The single most sattvic and tridoshic pulse. The foundation of Kitchari and the first solid food given after illness or fasting because it nourishes without creating Ama.
Sprouting raises the Prana and vitamin C content sharply while breaking down phytates. The intact skin adds fibre but also Vata, so hing and ginger are the traditional companions.
The everyday dal of most Indian households. Gas-forming for Vata constitutions unless cooked with hing, ajwain and enough ghee; excellent for cooling summer Pitta.
The fastest-cooking and most easily absorbed dal, breaking down to a light broth. Prescribed in convalescence when Agni is too weak for heavier pulses.
Balya and Vrishya — the strength-building pulse, traditionally given to wrestlers and to those recovering from Vata depletion. Heavy and Snigdha, so best fermented into idli or dosa.
Very low glycemic index, making it the preferred pulse in Ayurvedic diabetes regimens. Needs soaking and generous hing to keep it from aggravating Vata.
Substantial and satisfying, but Guru and Vatala. Always discard the soaking water and cook with ajwain, ginger and hing to make it Pathya.
Strongly Kapha-reducing and unusually iron-dense. The classic Naivedya offering of Navaratri and a staple of temple sundal, prepared without onion or garlic.
The heaviest of the common pulses and the most Vatala. Must be soaked 8 hours, cooked thoroughly, and spiced warm — undercooked kidney beans are genuinely toxic.
Ruksha and drying, which makes it the flour of choice for Kapha excess. Always paired with ajwain, which is the specific corrective for the bloating besan can cause.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Complete amino acid profile, Isoflavones, Lecithin

ayurvedic_properties.significance: By far the most protein-dense vegetarian ingredient in the pantry, but Guru and Abhishyandi in classical terms. Best at midday, well spiced, and in moderate rather than daily portions.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Complete protein, Isoflavones, Calcium sulfate, Manganese

ayurvedic_properties.significance: A cooling, dairy-free source of complete protein. Its Sheeta and Guru nature demands warming preparation — ginger, cumin, turmeric and dry heat rather than steaming.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Vitamin E, Magnesium, Riboflavin, Monounsaturated fats

ayurvedic_properties.significance: Medhya Rasayana — the classical brain and nerve tonic. Must be soaked overnight and peeled, as the skin is considered Pitta-aggravating and blocks absorption.
Guru and oily, building bulk quickly. Always roast and remove the skins, which are hard to digest, and moderate the quantity when Pitta is high.
The supreme Vata-pacifying seed and the highest plant calcium in this pantry. Central to Shishira (winter) foods and to the til-gud sweets of Makar Sankranti.
The most zinc-dense seed available and among the highest in plant protein. Traditionally used as a gentle anti-parasitic (Krimighna) and a support for the male reproductive tissue.
Snigdha and grounding, excellent for depleted Vata. Soaked and blended it makes a sattvic cream that replaces dairy in gravies without any onion or garlic.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Complete amino acid profile, Quercetin, Manganese, Magnesium

ayurvedic_properties.significance: Laghu and Ruksha, so it suits Kapha far better than rice or wheat. One of the few grains carrying all nine essential amino acids, making it a genuine standalone protein.
A Phalahara grain permitted during vrata and Navaratri. Rare among grains in retaining lysine, which makes it a complete protein and deeply Ojas-building cooked in milk.
The retained bran adds fibre and minerals but makes it Guru and slower to digest than white rice. Soak before cooking and pair with ghee so Vata is not disturbed.
Considered the most sattvic of grains — light, easily digested and never obstructing the channels. Aged basmati is preferred, as fresh new rice is held to be heavier and more Kaphakara.
A winter grain in the rural Deccan and Rajasthan for good reason — strongly heating and Kapha-clearing. Always eaten with ghee or white butter to offset its dryness.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Lutein, Folate, Vitamin K, Nitrates, Oxalates

ayurvedic_properties.significance: Rakta Shodhaka — a blood purifier and builder. Its oxalates bind calcium, so Ayurveda advises cooking rather than eating raw and avoiding it alongside large amounts of dairy.
Considered mildly Rajasic and acidic in classical terms. Cooking with turmeric and ghee tempers the sourness; strict sattvic kitchens reduce or omit it during Pitta-dominant seasons.
Vishwabheshaja, the universal medicine. A slice with rock salt before eating is the classical Agni-kindler; indispensable for making heavy pulses and dairy digestible.
Rajasic and stimulating rather than sattvic. Use sparingly and deseeded; in strict sattvic cooking black pepper or ginger is substituted for it entirely.
Tridoshic and cooling — the standard finish for any dish that has run hot with chilli or sour spice. Also traditionally used to help the body clear heavy metals.
Genuinely tridoshic and one of very few spices that aids digestion while actively cooling Pitta. Dhania water is the classic remedy for burning urination and acidity.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Ferulic acid, Umbelliferone, Volatile sulfur compounds

ayurvedic_properties.significance: The keystone of sattvic cooking — it delivers the savoury depth of onion and garlic without their Rajasic and Tamasic qualities. Must be bloomed in hot ghee to work.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Sodium chloride with trace magnesium, potassium and sulfur

ayurvedic_properties.significance: Saindhava lavana is named the best of all salts in the classical texts — the only one that does not aggravate Pitta or cause fluid retention, and the only salt permitted during vrata.
Deepana and Keshya — kindles digestion and is the classical hair tonic. Eat the leaves rather than pushing them aside; the calcium and carotenes are in the leaf, not the oil.
Strongly Kapha-dissolving and Ama-clearing. The seeds must pop fully in hot ghee — unpopped mustard stays raw and bitter and will sour the whole dish.
The great Pitta pacifier of the coastal south. Add it grated and fresh off the heat — frying destroys both its cooling virya and its delicate sweetness.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Citric acid, Vitamin C, Limonene, Potassium

ayurvedic_properties.significance: Ruchya — restores appetite and taste. Squeezed in raw at the table, its vitamin C converts plant iron into the absorbable form, which is why it belongs on every dal and green.
Unlike refined sugar, jaggery is warming and does not clog the channels. Old jaggery is classically described as light and cleansing; never add it to boiling milk or it will split.
Deepana and Vata-pacifying despite its bitterness. Long used in Ayurveda to steady blood sugar and support lactation; crush the dried leaves between the palms to release the aroma.
The specific remedy for gas and colic (Vatanulomana). Added to besan, chickpeas and kidney beans precisely because it neutralises the compounds in them that cause bloating.
Part of the Trijata group. Opens the circulatory channels (Srotoshodhana) and supports healthy blood sugar; a little goes far, as excess aggravates Pitta quickly.

pantry_ingredients.active_compounds: Cucurbitacins, Vitamin C, Potassium, high water content

ayurvedic_properties.significance: The lightest of all cooked vegetables and a staple of Pathya (therapeutic) diets. Always taste a raw sliver first — a bitter lauki contains toxic cucurbitacins and must be discarded.
Chakshushya — supports the eyes through its carotene, which needs ghee to be absorbed at all. Cooked carrot is markedly easier on Vata than raw.
